extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American political history and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating the distinctive standards, virtues, and failings attributed to Jeffersonian and Hamiltonian political thought (and their successors) as discussed in a book-chapter treatment of early American political development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of liberty and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jeffersonian error: an inability to discern wherein any antagonism existed between liberty and equality, and the extent to which they were sacrificing a desirable liberty to an undesirable equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware policies or doctrines that treat equality and liberty as automatically harmonious; evaluate whether efforts to secure equality in fact undermine 'positive' liberty (intellectual and moral achievement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of liberty by strong national organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine liberty could be protected only by an energetic and clear-sighted central government, and fertilized only by the efficient national organization of American activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a political order provides sufficient central organization and energetic leadership to secure and promote liberty in practice, not merely in constitutional declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of selection/classification under national organization
rubrics_metrics.description: National organization demands ... a certain amount of selection, and a certain classification of these individuals according to their abilities and deserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a proposed national system allows for appointment or recognition based on ability/merit and whether objections to such classification are principled or stem from distrust of social differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing intellectual and moral independence (vs conformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeffersonians showed an instinctive and implacable distrust of intellectual and moral independence, and have always sought to suppress it in favor of intellectual and moral conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging political cultures or policies, evaluate whether they encourage independent moral/intellectual initiative or enforce conformity under the guise of equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership must persistently will the national good and use intelligent means
rubrics_metrics.description: The only method whereby the good could prevail either in individual or social life was by persistently willing that it should prevail and by the adoption of intelligent means to that end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active, intentional, and intelligently planned public policy to fatalistic 'drift'; assess leaders on persistence and use of effective tools for public ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders should not be mere instruments of popular favor
rubrics_metrics.description: Jefferson courted popular favor and never used the influence obtained for the realization of any positive or formative purpose which might be unpopular; the leaders to whom the people delegated authority had in theory no right to pursue an unpopular policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether political leadership is willing to pursue necessary but unpopular reforms rather than simply doing what wins immediate popular approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism as political posture (preserving institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeffersonian policy was in all important respects merely a policy of conservatism: the political duty was confined to the administration of institutions in a faithful spirit and their preservation from harm; 'there was no room or need for any increase in the fund.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when political doctrine favors preservation and risk-aversion over reform or expansion; assess the risks of treating institutions as static stores to be guarded rather than developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy conceived as licensed individual selfishness
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic political system was considered tantamount in practice to a species of vigorous, licensed, and purified selfishness: responsibilities of government negative; those of the individual positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge democratic systems by whether they encourage only individual opportunism ('make hay while the sun is shining') or also collective responsibility and planned improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual integrity: aligning ideas and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Republicans tacitly admitted the substantial falsity of their attacks upon the Federal organization; instead of seriously considering the meaning of their own actions, they swallowed their past and shut their eyes—leading to intellectual lethargy, superficiality, and insincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political actors for consistency between professed principles and actual conduct; value candid revision of ideas or deliberate institutional reform over hypocrisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Union requires active maintenance (not drift)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union had been wrought by vigorous, responsible, and enterprising leadership; it was not to take care of itself and required active guardianship against perversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims that institutions will self-sustain; prioritize policies and leadership that actively sustain and improve national institutions rather than expect passive continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient national defense and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Republican superstition about militarism had prevented the formation of a regular army adequate to national policy and left the navy too small; lack of national organization made the War of 1812 humiliating reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing national policy, include readiness and institutional capacity for defense and international contingencies; avoid ideology that neglects practical preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming negative legal concepts into positive moral/social meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the alliance of liberty and union could be fruitful, both words had to be transformed from a negative and legal into a positive moral and social meaning (substituting 'democracy' for liberty and 'American nationality' for union).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating national doctrine, look for substantive moral and social content behind formal legal phrases; mere legal arrangements without underlying civic culture are precarious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that national consolidation can introduce hierarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: In a nationalized state, it is the man of exceptional position, power, responsibility, and training who is most likely to be representative and efficient, whereas in a thoroughly democratic state the average man was the representative citizen—the pioneers opposed nationalization for fear of hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the efficiency gains of centralization and professional leadership against the democratic ideal of equal standing; examine trade-offs honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate institutions by services rendered, not merely privileges held (National Bank case)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Bank enjoyed exceptional privileges because of the services it performed; its privileges were inseparable from the services and responsibilities it assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before condemning institutions for legal privileges, assess whether their privileges are proportionate to essential public services and how difficult those services are to replace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to concentration of wealth as political power ('Money Power')
rubrics_metrics.description: Western Democrats feared the possession of any special power by men of wealth; their crusade against the 'Money Power' meant money must not become a political power in a democratic state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging financial or corporate institutions, examine whether economic inequalities translate into special, inaccessible political or institutional advantages that undermine democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic distribution of offices vs administrative competence (spoils system)
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction of the spoils system aimed to share offices broadly as the political patrimony of the people, with short terms and rotation; yet it ultimately substituted one office-holding privilege for another and built professional politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess appointment and civil-service practices for the balance between democratic access and the need for trained, experienced administration; beware reforms that undermine competency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms should be constructive, not merely destructive
rubrics_metrics.description: The pioneers uprooted a national institution (the Bank) and altered civil-service tradition without considering whether its services could be substituted—attempted destructive innovations illustrate unconscious tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor reform proposals that provide replacements for essential functions; critique destructive reforms that remove institutions without planning alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciling opposing political traditions requires sacrifice and candidness
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption by Jefferson and the Republicans of the political structure of their opponents was an important practical indication that democracy and Federalism were not radically antagonistic, but the alliance was founded on a sacrifice by both parties of certain convictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating political settlements, recognize the legitimacy of compromise but also question whether the compromises involved intellectual surrender or candid adaptation of principles.
